OP, be sure you understand how the package manager works

Basically, most of the programs you will install will be in the Linux Mint repositories. These repositories exist as offline databases on your computer, that hold the information on how to obtain programs and what their newest versions are. To install a program from these repositories, for example Firefox, it would be "apt-get install firefox". If you don't know if a program is on the repositories, or want to find the name of the package you should install, type "apt-cache search firefox" (where, in this case you would be searching the repositories for Firefox)

Occasionally, the repositories on your computer will become out of date, so every day or so you should run "apt-get update" in order to provide your computer with information on what the newest versions of packages are and the up to date way of retrieving them should you want to install them. This shouldn't take more than a minute, as it's not actually updating any programs, just the big list of programs you can install.

To update all the programs and services running on your system, use the command "apt-get update" first to make sure all your repositories are up to date, and then to actually update all the programs on your computer, run "apt-get dist-upgrade". This one will take a while since it's upgrading every out of date program on your PC with the newest version.

Sometimes, packages will not be available on the package manager, but instead you'll find them on the internet as files ending in .deb , for example Steam is installed this way. The easiest way to install .deb packages is through the program " gdebi", which can be installed via apt-get. Simply open the .deb package in gdebi and it will help guide you through installing it.

That's how to use the package manager, do you want more tutorials on general Linux stuff?
